description: Teacher-approved OCR J277 five-lesson You Do pilot

questions.text: Explain why binary search requires the array to be sorted before searching.

scheme.point: The array must be in a known sorted order.
The comparison with the middle element then determines which half can safely be discarded.

questions.note: Saying “because it is faster” alone is insufficient.

questions.text: A sorted array has the values [2, 5, 8, 12, 16, 21, 27]. Show the steps of binary search for 21 using zero-based indices and midpoint = (low + high) DIV 2. Record the first midpoint, the updated search range and the midpoint at which 21 is found.

scheme.point: First midpoint index 3, value 12.
Since 21 > 12, update low to 4 (search indices 4–6).
New midpoint index 5, value 21; found at index 5.

questions.note: Accept a clear trace table or equivalent ordered steps.

questions.text: A sorted array has the values [3, 7, 11, 15, 19, 23, 27, 31, 35]. Show the steps of binary search for 8, starting with low = 0 and high = 8. Use midpoint = (low + high) DIV 2 and show the midpoint values checked. State the condition that ends the unsuccessful search.

scheme.point: mid = 4; value 19; set high = 3.
mid = 1; value 7; set low = 2.
mid = 2; value 11; set high = 1.
low (2) > high (1), so the target is absent and the search ends.

questions.note: Zero-based indexing and integer division. Do not award a final index for an absent target.

questions.text: State two environmental impacts of frequently replacing working school laptops.

scheme.point: Electronic waste from discarded devices.
Use of energy/raw materials and resulting emissions during manufacture.

questions.note: Also accept other distinct valid environmental impacts; do not credit repeats.

questions.text: A school uses an online-only parent communication app. Explain one way this could disadvantage some families and one practical step the school could take to reduce that problem.

scheme.point: Identify the disadvantage: some families have poor connectivity, lack devices or need accessible alternatives.
Explain how that prevents timely access to homework, attendance messages or school information.
Give a relevant mitigation, such as printed letters, phone calls, translation or accessible formats.

questions.note: Any coherent supported disadvantage and matched response can earn full marks.

questions.text: A multi-academy trust plans to replace printed letters with a compulsory online-only system for homework, attendance and communication with parents. Discuss the ethical, cultural and environmental implications of this proposal. You should consider different viewpoints and reach a supported conclusion.

scheme.point: No relevant response.
Limited relevant knowledge; simple or unconnected points, little application to the trust.
Some developed discussion of benefits and drawbacks linked to the scenario; partial balance and a basic judgement.
Well-developed, balanced argument addressing ethical/cultural and environmental implications, applied to the trust; clear reasoned conclusion.

indicative: Advantages: faster communication, accessible records and potentially less printing, delivery and paper waste.
Ethical/cultural concerns: digital exclusion, accessibility needs, language barriers, privacy of pupil/family data, unequal access.
Environmental trade-offs: reduced paper/travel versus electricity, devices, manufacturing emissions and electronic waste.
Reasoned decision: adopt digital by default but preserve accessible paper, telephone or translated routes and protect personal data.
questions.note: Teacher-generated indicative levels, not copied from OCR’s official mark scheme. Assess the whole response; do not add one mark per bullet.

questions.text: State what is meant by input and output in a computer program.

scheme.point: Input: data received by a program, for example entered by a user.
Output: information produced by the program, for example displayed on screen.

questions.note: Two distinct definitions: do not award two marks for examples alone.

questions.text: A cinema sells tickets for £6 each. A customer chooses how many tickets to buy. Describe how input, processing and output would be used to display the total cost.

scheme.point: Input: obtain the number of tickets from the customer.
Processing: multiply the number by £6 to calculate the total.
Output: display the calculated total to the customer.

questions.note: Accept equivalent wording tied to the stated ticket scenario.

questions.text: Tickets for a school concert cost £6 each. Write OCR Exam Reference Language instructions to assign the ticket price, input the number of tickets as an integer, calculate the total cost and print the total.

scheme.point: Correct assignment of price: ticketPrice = 6.
An integer input is stored: tickets = int(input("Number of tickets?"))
Total is calculated by multiplication: total = ticketPrice * tickets.
The total is output: print(total).

questions.model_code:
ticketPrice = 6
tickets = int(input("Number of tickets?"))
total = ticketPrice * tickets
print(total)
questions.note: An equivalent OCR ERL solution with valid variable names earns the same marks. Do not deduct for harmless prompt wording.

questions.text: A school represents pupil records in a two-dimensional array. State what a row and a column represent in this table.

scheme.point: Each row represents one pupil (one record).
Each column represents one field, e.g. name or tutor group.

questions.note: OCR J277 explicitly permits 2D arrays to emulate records and data tables.

questions.text: A school stores pupil names and tutor groups in a two-dimensional array called pupils. Explain how rows, columns and indices could be used to find the tutor group for a particular pupil.

scheme.point: A row represents a particular pupil.
A column represents the field required, here the tutor group.
Use the chosen row and column indices to access that value, e.g. pupils[1,1].

questions.note: Assume zero-based indices and column 1 = tutor group, as shown in Code First.

questions.text: A school uses a two-dimensional array where column 0 stores a pupil name and column 1 stores the tutor group. Write OCR Exam Reference Language statements to declare an array with two rows and two columns, store "Ben" and "10B" in the second row, then print that pupil’s tutor group.

scheme.point: array pupils[2,2] declared.
pupils[1,0] = "Ben" sets the second pupil name.
pupils[1,1] = "10B" sets the tutor group.
print(pupils[1,1]) prints the correct indexed field.

questions.note: OCR ERL only; a 2D array emulates the record fields.

096.title: Primary Storage: RAM, ROM and Cache

questions.text: State which of RAM and ROM is volatile and which is non-volatile.

scheme.point: RAM is volatile.
ROM is non-volatile.

questions.note: Exact terminology matters.

questions.text: A pupil uses several applications on a laptop. Explain how cache memory can help the CPU run programs efficiently.

scheme.point: Cache holds frequently or recently used data and instructions.
The CPU can retrieve these more quickly than from main RAM.
This reduces waiting for memory access and may improve overall performance.

questions.note: Avoid claiming that cache makes every program automatically faster.

questions.text: A school is choosing between two otherwise identical laptops. Laptop A has 4 GB RAM; Laptop B has 8 GB RAM. Pupils regularly run applications that together need about 6 GB of working memory. Justify which laptop is more suitable, including one limitation of upgrading RAM alone.

scheme.point: Select Laptop B (8 GB).
Explain that 8 GB can accommodate the stated 6 GB working-memory demand.
Laptop A may rely more heavily on virtual memory, which is slower than RAM.
Acknowledge that CPU/storage or other bottlenecks can still limit performance despite extra RAM.

questions.note: Accept equivalent technically accurate justifications. The scenario fixes other specifications to isolate RAM.

questions.text: A school stores pupilName = "Amira" and visits = 3. State the most suitable data type for each variable. [2 marks]

scheme.point: pupilName: string (text).
visits: integer (whole-number count).

questions.note: Award each independent marking point once; credit equivalent accurate OCR ERL.

questions.text: A club starts with visits = 2, then runs visits = visits + 1 and print(visits). Explain the new stored value and the output. [3 marks]

scheme.point: Original value of visits is 2.
The assignment updates visits to 3 by adding 1.
Output is 3, because print uses the new value.

questions.note: Award each independent marking point once; credit equivalent accurate OCR ERL.

questions.text: A school club logs visits. Write OCR ERL to input a pupil name and an integer number of visits, increase visits by one, then display the pupil name and updated count. [4 marks]

scheme.point: Input and store the pupil name in a variable.
Input the visit count and cast it to integer.
Increase the stored visit count by 1.
Display both the pupil name and the updated count.

questions.model_code:
name = input("Pupil name?")
visits = int(input("Visits?"))
visits = visits + 1
print(name)
print(visits)
questions.note: Award each independent marking point once; credit equivalent accurate OCR ERL.

questions.text: Calculate (a) 17 DIV 5 and (b) 17 MOD 5. [2 marks]

scheme.point: 17 DIV 5 = 3 (whole-number quotient).
17 MOD 5 = 2 (remainder).

questions.note: Award each independent marking point once; credit equivalent accurate OCR ERL.

questions.text: The input function returns the text "4". Explain why a program must cast this value before adding it to the integer 6. Include the numeric result. [3 marks]

scheme.point: The input is initially a string/text value.
Casting with int() converts suitable numeric text to an integer.
4 + 6 gives the numeric result 10.

questions.note: Award each independent marking point once; credit equivalent accurate OCR ERL.

questions.text: A cycle-hire company charges £5 for every hour plus a £3 fixed booking fee. Write OCR ERL to input the number of hours, calculate the bill and display it. [4 marks]

scheme.point: Input the duration and convert it to integer.
Multiply hours by 5 to find the hourly charge.
Add the fixed booking fee of 3 exactly once.
Display the calculated total.

questions.note: Award each independent marking point once; credit equivalent accurate OCR ERL.

questions.text: A visitor has age = 16 and hasTicket = false. State the results of (age >= 18 AND hasTicket) and (age < 18 OR hasTicket). [2 marks]

scheme.point: First expression evaluates to false.
Second expression evaluates to true, since age < 18.

questions.note: Award each independent marking point once; credit equivalent accurate OCR ERL.

questions.text: A sports club admits someone only when they are a registered member AND their subscription is paid. Explain why AND is suitable rather than OR. [3 marks]

scheme.point: Membership must be true to admit a visitor.
Paid subscription must also be true.
AND requires both conditions; OR could admit someone with only one of them.

questions.note: Award each independent marking point once; credit equivalent accurate OCR ERL.

questions.text: A museum permits entry when a visitor is at least 16 AND has a ticket, OR has a staff pass. Write OCR ERL using age, hasTicket and hasPass to display "Enter" or "Wait". [4 marks]

scheme.point: Correct age comparison age >= 16.
Combine age and ticket using AND.
Allow the staff-pass alternative using OR and suitable grouping.
Use IF/ELSE and output the matching message.

questions.model_code:
if (age >= 16 AND hasTicket) OR hasPass then
    print("Enter")
else
    print("Wait")
endif
questions.note: Award each independent marking point once; credit equivalent accurate OCR ERL.

questions.text: State what happens to instructions inside an IF block when its condition is (a) true and (b) false. [2 marks]

scheme.point: When true, instructions inside the IF block run.
When false, those instructions are skipped.

questions.note: Award each independent marking point once; credit equivalent accurate OCR ERL.

questions.text:
A program runs:
score = 47
if score >= 50 then
    print("Pass")
endif
print("Finished")
Explain the output. [3 marks]

scheme.point: 47 >= 50 evaluates to false.
The IF block is skipped so Pass is not printed.
Finished is printed after ENDIF.

questions.note: Award each independent marking point once; credit equivalent accurate OCR ERL.

questions.text: Cinema tickets cost £8 for children under 16 and £12 otherwise. Write OCR ERL to input an age, select the correct price and display it. [4 marks]

scheme.point: Input age and cast it to an integer.
Use the condition age < 16 in an IF statement.
Assign 8 for under-16s and 12 for everyone else.
Display the selected price after the IF/ELSE.

questions.model_code:
age = int(input("Age?"))
if age < 16 then
    price = 8
else
    price = 12
endif
print(price)
questions.note: Award each independent marking point once; credit equivalent accurate OCR ERL.

questions.text: A program applies these conditions in order: age < 5, age < 18, otherwise. State which branch is selected for ages 4 and 12. [2 marks]

scheme.point: Age 4 selects the first (under 5) branch.
Age 12 selects the second (under 18) branch.

questions.note: Award each independent marking point once; credit equivalent accurate OCR ERL.

questions.text: A museum charges different prices for under-5s, 5–17s and adults. Explain why one IF/ELSEIF/ELSE chain is preferable to three independent IF statements. [3 marks]

scheme.point: The conditions are checked in a defined order.
Once a branch matches, the remaining alternatives are skipped.
This avoids multiple price assignments for the same visitor.

questions.note: Award each independent marking point once; credit equivalent accurate OCR ERL.

questions.text: Museum entry is free under age 5, £4 for ages 5–17, and £9 for adults. Write OCR ERL to choose and display the price for an integer variable age. [4 marks]

scheme.point: Test age < 5 and assign price 0.
Use ELSEIF age < 18 for the 5–17 group.
Use ELSE to assign price 9 for adults.
Close with ENDIF and display the selected price.

questions.model_code:
if age < 5 then
    price = 0
elseif age < 18 then
    price = 4
else
    price = 9
endif
print(price)
questions.note: Award each independent marking point once; credit equivalent accurate OCR ERL.

questions.text:
The code runs:
for i = 1 to 5
    print(i)
next i
State the first number and the last number printed. [2 marks]

scheme.point: First printed number is 1.
Last printed number is 5.

questions.note: Award each independent marking point once; credit equivalent correct responses.

questions.text:
A school totals points using:
total = 0
for i = 1 to 3
    total = total + i
next i
Show the value of total after each iteration. [3 marks]

scheme.point: After i = 1, total is 1.
After i = 2, total is 3.
After i = 3, total is 6.

questions.note: Award each independent marking point once; credit equivalent correct responses.

questions.text: A cinema sells exactly four tickets, each costing £6. Write OCR ERL using a FOR loop to calculate and display the total price. [4 marks]

scheme.point: Initialise total to 0.
Use FOR to repeat four times.
Add 6 to total on each iteration.
Close the loop and print total.

questions.model_code:
total = 0
for i = 1 to 4
    total = total + 6
next i
print(total)
questions.note: Award each independent marking point once; credit equivalent correct responses.

questions.text: The loop begins with count = 0 and repeats while count < 3, adding 1 to count each time. State the number of iterations and final value of count. [2 marks]

scheme.point: The loop runs 3 times.
The final value of count is 3.

questions.note: Award each independent marking point once; credit equivalent correct responses.

questions.text: A school login program keeps asking for a PIN until the correct PIN is entered. Explain why a WHILE loop is suitable and how it eventually stops. [3 marks]

scheme.point: The number of attempts is not known in advance.
WHILE checks the continuation condition before each attempt.
A new input updates the tested value so the loop can end when the PIN is correct.

questions.note: Award each independent marking point once; credit equivalent correct responses.

questions.text: A school club accepts a score from 0 to 10 inclusive. Write OCR ERL to read a score, ask again while it is out of range, and display "Accepted" when valid. [4 marks]

scheme.point: Input score as an integer before the loop.
Continue the WHILE loop when score < 0 OR score > 10.
Re-read the score inside the loop.
End the loop and print Accepted.

questions.model_code:
score = int(input("Score?"))
while score < 0 OR score > 10
    score = int(input("Try again:"))
endwhile
print("Accepted")
questions.note: Award each independent marking point once; credit equivalent correct responses.

questions.text: A program starts with total = 2, then executes total = total + 3 followed by total = total * 2. State total after each assignment. [2 marks]

scheme.point: After adding 3, total is 5.
After multiplying by 2, total is 10.

questions.note: Award each independent marking point once; credit equivalent correct responses.

questions.text:
A school program executes:
points = 4
if points > 5 then
    points = points + 1
else
    points = points + 3
endif
points = points * 2
print(points)
Show points after the IF/ELSE, after the multiplication, and at output. [3 marks]

scheme.point: After IF/ELSE: points = 7 because 4 > 5 is false and 4 + 3 = 7.
After multiplication: points = 14.
Printed result is 14.

questions.note: Award each independent marking point once; credit equivalent correct responses.

questions.text:
A fitness app executes:
count = 0
for i = 1 to 4
    if i MOD 2 == 0 then
        count = count + 1
    endif
next i
print(count)
Show how count changes during iteration and include the printed value. [4 marks]

scheme.point: For i = 1 and i = 3 the condition is false, so count does not change.
For i = 2, count increases from 0 to 1.
For i = 4, count increases from 1 to 2.
The printed result is 2.

questions.note: Award each independent marking point once; credit equivalent correct responses.

questions.text: A school program repeats inputting a test mark and uses IF to check whether the mark is at least 50. Identify the two control-flow constructs used. [2 marks]

scheme.point: Iteration for repeated input.
Selection for the IF condition.

questions.note: Award each independent marking point once; credit equivalent correct responses.

questions.text: A charity records donations until a volunteer enters 0. Explain how sequence and iteration would work together in this program. [3 marks]

scheme.point: An initial input is read before checking the loop condition.
Iteration repeats the input and processing while the sentinel 0 has not been entered.
Input is updated each iteration so the loop eventually stops when 0 is entered.

questions.note: Award each independent marking point once; credit equivalent correct responses.

questions.text: A teacher enters three test marks. Write OCR ERL using a loop and an IF statement to count and display how many marks are at least 80. [4 marks]

scheme.point: Initialise the counter to 0.
Use FOR to input three marks, converting to integer.
Use IF mark >= 80 to increment the counter.
Close the loop and print the counter.

questions.model_code:
count = 0
for i = 1 to 3
    mark = int(input("Mark?"))
    if mark >= 80 then
        count = count + 1
    endif
next i
print(count)
questions.note: Award each independent marking point once; credit equivalent correct responses.
